title: Harvard Mark I and the Bell Labs relay computers
text:
CHAPTER 2. RELAYS AND ELECTROMECHANICAL COMPUTERS
SECTION 2.4. HARVARD MARK I AND THE BELL LABS RELAY COMPUTERS

Zuse worked alone in Berlin. In the United States, two quite different relay computing projects grew up in the late 1930s: one at Bell Telephone Laboratories, starting from a binary adder built on a kitchen table, and one at Harvard, where a physics graduate student persuaded IBM to build a giant program-controlled calculator. Together they show the strengths and the hard limits of electromechanical computing, and they trained people, such as Grace Hopper, who went on to shape the software era.

1. George Stibitz and the Model K (1937)

George Stibitz (1904-1995) was a mathematician working at Bell Labs in New York, the research arm of the American telephone system. Bell Labs had enormous experience with relays, because the automatic telephone exchange was essentially a giant relay network. In November 1937 Stibitz took some surplus telephone relays home and built a small relay adder that added two one-bit binary numbers and showed the result on lamps. He later called it the "Model K," after the kitchen table on which he reportedly assembled it. Replicas are held by the Computer History Museum and the Smithsonian, among others.

Technically the Model K is just the half adder of Section 2.2:

    S = A XOR B
    C = A AND B

realized with relay contacts, with the inputs set by switches (Stibitz used strips of metal cut from a tobacco can, according to accounts of the device) and the outputs shown on flashlight bulbs. Its importance was not its capability but the demonstration, to Bell Labs management, that relays wired as binary logic could do arithmetic.

2. The Complex Number Calculator (1939-1940)

Bell Labs engineers spent a great deal of time on calculations with complex numbers, which are central to the analysis of AC circuits and filters (impedances such as Z = R + jX). Stibitz, working with switching engineer Samuel Williams, designed a relay machine to multiply and divide complex numbers. The Complex Number Calculator (CNC), later called the Bell Labs Model I, was completed in November 1939 and put into operation in 1940.

Some design features worth noting:

  - It used a binary-coded decimal scheme internally (Stibitz used an "excess-3" code, in which each decimal digit d is represented by the 4-bit binary value of d + 3). Excess-3 has a useful property: the 9's complement of a digit, needed for subtraction, is obtained simply by inverting all four bits. Check it: digit 2 is 0101; inverting gives 1010 = 10, which is 7 + 3, the code for 7, and 9 - 2 = 7.
  - It was operated from teletype terminals, so users typed problems and received printed answers.

Remote computing, 1940. In September 1940, at a meeting of the American Mathematical Society and the Mathematical Association of America at Dartmouth College in Hanover, New Hampshire, Stibitz demonstrated the CNC by sending problems from a modified teletype in Hanover over telegraph lines to the machine in New York, with the answers returned the same way. This is often cited as the first demonstration of remote access to a computing machine, the distant ancestor of time-sharing, terminals and cloud computing. Among the audience, according to many historical accounts, were John Mauchly, later co-designer of ENIAC, and Norbert Wiener, later founder of cybernetics (Chapter 7).

During and after the war Bell Labs built a series of further relay machines (Models II through VI), several for military fire-control and ballistics work. The later ones were quite sophisticated, with features such as floating point and extensive self-checking. Stibitz is often credited with introducing the word "digital" for this kind of computation, in contrast to analog machines.

3. Howard Aiken and the Harvard Mark I

Howard Aiken (1900-1973) was a physics graduate student at Harvard in the 1930s whose research required tedious numerical solution of differential equations. In 1937 he wrote a proposal for a large-scale automatic calculating machine. He knew of Babbage's work and is reported to have been impressed by a fragment of a Babbage engine held at Harvard. After the proposal was rejected by others (including a calculator company), it was taken up by IBM, then the leading maker of punched-card tabulating equipment, with the support of its chairman Thomas J. Watson.

IBM engineers, notably Clair Lake, Frank Hamilton and Benjamin Durfee, built the machine at IBM's plant in Endicott, New York. IBM called it the Automatic Sequence Controlled Calculator (ASCC); Harvard called it the Mark I. It was shipped to Harvard in February 1944, began computing for the US Navy Bureau of Ships in May, and was officially presented to the university on August 7, 1944. (A public dispute over credit followed: Harvard's press release emphasized Aiken, which IBM resented, and relations between Aiken and IBM soured.)

4. What the Mark I was like

Physically it was enormous: a steel frame about 51 feet (15.5 m) long and 8 feet (2.4 m) high, about 2 feet deep, containing around 765,000 electromechanical components and about 500 miles of wire. Its parts included roughly 3,500 relays, rotating shafts, clutches, and counter wheels derived from IBM tabulator technology. A 50-foot drive shaft along the bottom, turned by a 5-horsepower electric motor, kept all the units synchronized and served as the system clock. Observers often described the noise of the machine in operation as like a roomful of knitting needles or typewriters.

Number representation. The Mark I was decimal. It had 72 accumulating registers ("counters"), each storing a signed 23-digit decimal number, plus 60 registers of constants set by hand with banks of rotary switches. A digit was stored by the angular position of a ten-position counter wheel, essentially the same principle as a mechanical adding machine: adding means rotating a wheel by the right number of steps, with mechanical carry to the next wheel.

Speed (commonly quoted figures):

    addition or subtraction: about 0.3 s (three per second)
    multiplication:          about 6 s
    division:                about 15.3 s
    logarithm or trig function: over a minute

Compare these with the Z3 (addition about 0.8 s, multiplication about 3 s, but only about 4 to 5 significant digits) and you see the trade-off: Aiken's machine carried far more precision (23 digits) and was more robust in operation, but was much bigger.

5. Programming the Mark I

Instructions were read from a 24-channel punched paper tape. Each instruction line had fields specifying, roughly, where the result should go, where the operand came from, and what operation to perform. Data came from punched cards, from the hand-set switch registers, or from other tapes; results were printed on electric typewriters or punched on cards.

The Mark I, like the Z3, had no conditional branch in its original form. Loops were made by literally gluing the end of the program tape to its beginning, or by writing the instructions out repeatedly ("unrolling" the loop). Conditional choices were made at first by the human operators, who stopped the machine and switched tapes. Later modifications added a facility for conditional operation. Because instructions came from tape and data lived in counters, instructions and data were physically separate; modern writers sometimes call this a "Harvard architecture," though historians point out the term was coined much later and fits Aiken's later machines better than the Mark I itself.

A typical problem: the Mark I computed large tables of mathematical functions such as Bessel functions, which are needed for problems in wave propagation, vibration and heat flow. Operators nicknamed the machine "Bessy, the Bessel engine." Harvard published the results as a series of volumes of tables.

6. Grace Hopper and early programming culture

Grace Murray Hopper (1906-1992), a mathematician with a Yale PhD and a US Navy Reserve officer, was assigned to the Mark I project in 1944 and became one of its first programmers. With Aiken and the crew she wrote the machine's manual, A Manual of Operation for the Automatic Sequence Controlled Calculator (1946), one of the first detailed accounts of programming a computer.

Several habits of later software engineering appear in the Harvard group's work: libraries of reusable tape sequences for common calculations (an early form of subroutines), careful documentation, and systematic checking. The Mark I also did war work. One of the first programs run on it, begun on 29 March 1944, was set up by John von Neumann for the Manhattan Project, to study whether implosion was a viable way to detonate an atomic bomb.

The bug story. A famous logbook from the Harvard Mark II, the relay successor machine, contains an entry from September 1947 with a moth taped to the page and the note "First actual case of bug being found." The moth had been found in a relay. The word "bug" for a technical fault was already in engineering use long before (it is attested in Thomas Edison's time), which is exactly why the entry is a joke: this was an actual insect. The logbook page is held by the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History. Hopper often told the story, though she did not write the entry herself.

Hopper went on to UNIVAC and to compilers: her A-0 system of the early 1950s is among the first compilers, and her FLOW-MATIC language strongly influenced COBOL.

7. Aiken's later machines

Aiken built a succession of machines at Harvard: the Mark II (completed around 1947-1948, still relay-based but faster), the Mark III (1949, mostly electronic, using vacuum tubes and crystal diodes with magnetic drum storage) and the Mark IV (1952). The Mark I itself was taken apart in 1959; parts went to IBM, the Smithsonian and Harvard's Collection of Historical Scientific Instruments, where a large section is on display.

Aiken also founded one of the first academic computing programs, at Harvard, and trained many early computer scientists. He was, however, skeptical of the stored-program approach and of how many computers the world would need. A frequently repeated quotation claiming he said only a handful of computers would ever be needed in the United States is of uncertain wording and provenance, so this book does not quote it.

8. Why relays lost

By 1944, when the Mark I went into service, the electromechanical approach was already reaching its limits. The reasons give a good engineering summary of what any switching technology must provide.

  Speed. A relay contact moves physically. Mechanical inertia, spring forces and contact bounce limit switching to milliseconds. Even the best relays could not switch much faster than around a thousand times a second, and practical machines ran far slower. A vacuum tube switches electrons with no moving parts, in microseconds or less, roughly a thousand times or more faster.

  Wear and reliability. Contacts arc, pit and wear out, and dust (or moths) can stop them. A machine with thousands of relays needs constant maintenance, though, interestingly, relay machines could be quite dependable in daily use because faults tended to be intermittent rather than catastrophic.

  Size and power. Each relay is a coil, an armature and contacts; a computer needs thousands to millions of switching events per operation.

The decisive demonstration came in 1946, when ENIAC (Section 4.3) showed electronic computation running on the order of a thousand times faster than electromechanical machines. Yet relays did not disappear from engineering. They remain in power switching, safety interlocks and industrial control panels, and, as discussed in Section 2.1, the logic of relay panels lives on in the ladder diagrams of PLCs.

9. The relay era in perspective

Between 1937 and the mid-1940s, three independent groups (Zuse in Germany, Stibitz and Williams at Bell Labs, Aiken and IBM at Harvard) built program-controlled relay or electromechanical calculators. They differed in number system (binary versus decimal), precision, size and purpose, but they shared crucial features:

  - arithmetic reduced to switching logic (Shannon's insight made practical);
  - automatic sequencing from an external punched program tape;
  - separate storage and arithmetic units;
  - no, or only primitive, conditional branching, and no stored program.

The missing pieces, electronic speed and a program held in memory like data, are the subject of Chapter 4. Before that, Chapter 3 goes back to theory: in 1936, before any of these machines ran, Alan Turing had already defined what it means for a machine to compute, and proved what no machine can do.

10. Summary

  - Stibitz's Model K (1937) was a kitchen-table relay binary adder; his Complex Number Calculator (completed 1939, in operation 1940) was demonstrated remotely by teletype from Dartmouth to New York in September 1940.
  - Aiken's Harvard Mark I (IBM ASCC), proposed in 1937, built by IBM in Endicott and presented on August 7, 1944, was 51 feet long with about 765,000 components, worked in 23-digit decimal, and did an addition in about 0.3 s and a multiplication in about 6 s.
  - It read instructions from punched paper tape and initially had no conditional branching; loops were made by joining tape ends.
  - Grace Hopper was one of its first programmers; the famous 1947 moth was found in the Mark II.
  - Relays were limited by mechanical speed, wear and size; vacuum tubes would replace them for computing.
